concept: Compound interest as a geometric sequence
prompt:
\$1000 is invested at a nominal annual interest rate of 6%.

**(a)** Explain why the values of the investment at the end of each year form a geometric sequence when interest is compounded annually. **[1]**

**(b)** Explain, without calculating, why compounding the same nominal rate monthly gives a larger value after one year. **[2]**
markscheme:
**(a)** Each year the value is multiplied by the same factor $1.06$, so consecutive values have a constant ratio. **(R1)**

**(b)** With monthly compounding, interest is added each month **(R1)** and later interest is earned on interest already added, so the effective yearly factor $\left(1+\tfrac{0.06}{12}\right)^{12}\approx1.0617$ exceeds $1.06$ **(R1)**.

prompt:
Priya invests \$5000 at a nominal annual interest rate of 4.2%, compounded monthly.

**(a)** Find the value of the investment after 6 years, to the nearest cent. **[3]**

**(b)** Find how long it takes for the investment to first exceed \$8000. Give your answer in years and months. **[3]**
markscheme:
**(a)** Monthly rate $\dfrac{4.2}{12}=0.35\%$ and $6\times12=72$ periods **(M1)**

$FV=5000(1.0035)^{72}$ **(M1)** $=\$6430.15$ **(A1)**

**(b)** $5000(1.0035)^{n}>8000 \iff 1.0035^{n}>1.6$ **(M1)**

$n>\dfrac{\ln1.6}{\ln1.0035}\approx134.5$, so $n=135$ months **(A1)** $=11$ years 3 months **(A1)**

(A TVM solver gives the same result: $N\approx134.5$.)

**Common mistake:** using $4.2\%$ with $n=72$ — the rate per period must match the number of periods.

prompt:
A car bought for \$28 000 depreciates by 15% each year.

**(a)** Find its value after 5 years. **[2]**

**(b)** Find the number of complete years after which the car's value first falls below \$10 000. **[2]**
markscheme:
**(a)** Each year the value is multiplied by $0.85$: $28000(0.85)^{5}$ **(M1)** $=\$12\,423.75$ **(A1)**

**(b)** $28000(0.85)^{n}<10000 \iff n>\dfrac{\ln(10000/28000)}{\ln0.85}\approx6.34$ **(M1)**, so after **7** years **(A1)**.

**Common mistake:** multiplying by $0.15$ — that is the amount lost, not the value kept.
